title: Teacher-to-classroom assignment and student achievement
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student achievement can be improved by changing which teachers teach which classrooms, without hiring new teachers or changing the overall teacher workforce. The authors focus on whether teacher effectiveness interacts with student and peer characteristics, such that alternative teacher-to-classroom assignments could raise average achievement relative to the status quo.

The study uses data from the Measures of Effective Teaching (MET) project in U.S. elementary and middle schools. Teachers were randomly assigned to classrooms within school-by-grade-by-subject blocks, and the authors use pre-experiment teacher observation scores from the Danielson Framework for Teaching (FFT) along with students’ baseline test scores to estimate how different assignments would affect outcomes. Because the realized experiment involved non-compliance and some student movement, the paper develops a semiparametric instrumental-variables approach to recover counterfactual average reallocation effects.

The sample includes grades 4–8 in math and English language arts across six large urban school districts. The main conclusion is that reassignment policies based on observed teacher quality and student achievement can produce modest but meaningful gains in average student test scores, on the order of 0.02 to 0.04 standard deviations. The authors conclude that teacher assignment is a potentially important, resource-neutral lever for improving achievement, though they note the results are provisional and may not generalize beyond the MET context.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical economics paper with a strong quasi-experimental/experimental foundation, but it is not a clean RCT of the policy of interest. The design relies on the MET experiment plus additional identifying assumptions and IV corrections for non-compliance, so credibility is meaningful but not fully gold-standard for the reallocation policy itself.
impact_tier_rationale: The estimated gains are modest in size (about 0.02 to 0.04 SD) and pertain to institutional teacher-assignment policy rather than a direct instructional intervention. The effects are potentially meaningful at scale, but they are not large enough to warrant a higher impact tier.

finding.finding_summary: The paper estimates that alternative teacher-to-classroom assignments could raise average student achievement in K-12 math and ELA, even without changing the teacher workforce. Using the MET experiment and a semiparametric IV approach, the authors report that an optimal reassignment could increase average classroom achievement by as much as 0.04 standard deviations, with the more realistic comparison to the status quo yielding about a 0.02 SD gain.
finding.measure: End-of-year standardized state test scores (z-scores) in mathematics and English language arts; average classroom student achievement under counterfactual teacher assignments
finding.study_size: math n≈8,500 students and 614 teachers; ELA n≈9,600 students and 649 teachers
finding.effect_size: 0.04 SD maximum gain; 0.02 SD status-quo-to-optimal gain

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates the institutional effect of changing within-school and within-district teacher assignment policies, showing that resource-neutral reassignment can meaningfully improve achievement. The authors characterize these reallocation effects as policy-relevant and note that optimal reassignment across existing classrooms can outperform the observed status quo without hiring additional teachers.
finding.measure: Counterfactual average reallocation effects from teacher assignment policies; optimal vs. status quo aggregate achievement
finding.study_size: math n≈8,500 students and 614 teachers; ELA n≈9,600 students and 649 teachers
finding.effect_size: 0.02-0.04 SD improvement in average test scores
